planting.note: Set divisions or rooted cuttings in humus-rich, constantly moist soil tucked against damp rock or at the base of a seep; it spreads slowly by trailing stems that root as they go.

directions: Rock skullcap is a low, trailing mint-family perennial found on wet rock ledges, streambanks, and seepage slopes in the Blue Ridge from Virginia to Georgia. Square stems creep over moss and damp stone before rising a few inches to produce loose racemes of blue-violet, two-lipped flowers from early to late summer. In cultivation it wants the same conditions it has in the wild: shaded, humid, perpetually damp rocky or gravelly soil, making it a good match for a shaded bog garden edge or a moss-and-stone seep feature. It is uncommon in the trade but increasingly offered by regional native plant nurseries propagating from cutting-grown stock.

planting.note: Start seed indoors on a bright windowsill since it needs light to germinate, then transplant into saturated, mucky soil at a seep edge or stream margin after frost danger passes.

directions: Winged monkeyflower grows in mountain seeps, swampy woods, and streambank mud throughout the Southern Appalachians, distinguished from the more widespread Allegheny monkeyflower by its angled, winged stems and distinctly stalked (petiolate) leaves. From mid to late summer it bears violet-blue, snapdragon-shaped flowers with a pale, dotted throat that attract bumblebees. It thrives where other perennials rot, tolerating standing water and heavy shade at a woodland seep, and is a reliable short-lived perennial that self-sows modestly when conditions stay wet.

planting.note: Plant rooted stolon sections directly into cold, mucky seep soil or shallow flowing water; it will not tolerate drying out even briefly, so a constant spring or seep source is essential.

directions: Mountain watercress forms loose mats of rounded, glossy leaves rooted directly in the cold, mineral-rich mud of mountain spring seeps and streamhead flushes across the Southern Appalachians. Clusters of small white, four-petaled flowers appear in early spring before the forest canopy fully closes. Unlike most garden perennials it is happiest with its roots in actively flowing, near-freezing seep water, making it a specialist choice for a constructed bog or spring-fed garden feature rather than ordinary moist soil. It spreads by rooting stolons and is best propagated by division of these runners in spring or fall.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in early spring and set into rich, perpetually moist soil along a shaded streambank or seep; established plants tolerate brief flooding.

directions: Drooping sedge grows in loose, arching clumps along shaded Southern Appalachian streambanks and seep margins, often rooted right at the waterline where seeping groundwater keeps the soil saturated year-round. Its narrow, gracefully pendent seed spikes dangle on thin stalks in late spring, giving the clump a fountain-like texture that pairs well with ferns and sedges in a naturalistic shade garden. It is an easy, long-lived perennial once established in consistently wet, humus-rich soil and spreads slowly by short rhizomes rather than aggressively seeding.

planting.note: Divide small tussocks in spring and plant into acidic, saturated, nutrient-poor soil such as sphagnum-rich bog mud; keep consistently wet, as it will not tolerate drying.

directions: Bristle-stalked sedge is a delicate, fine-textured sedge forming small soft tussocks in Southern Appalachian mountain bogs, fens, and seepage slopes, usually growing among sphagnum moss in highly acidic, nutrient-poor saturated soil. Its thread-like leaves and sparse, nearly hidden flower spikes give it a quiet, mossy presence rather than showy impact, but it adds authentic texture to a naturalistic bog planting alongside sundews and cranberry. It is easy to grow once sited correctly in a constantly wet, acidic bog garden, though it is intolerant of fertilizer or drying soil and is best left undisturbed once established.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)
